Statins can help to lower low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol in the blood.
Having a high level of LDL cholesterol can be dangerous. It can lead to the arteries becoming hard and narrow (atherosclerosis) and
cardiovascular disease (CVD)
.
Statins are only available with a prescription.
What are statins used for?
Cardiovascular disease (CVD)
is a general term that describes a disease of the heart or blood vessels.
Statins can’t cure CVD but they can help to:
stop it from getting worse
prevent it from reoccurring
reduce the chance of it developing in the first place in people at risk
Statins can also be used to treat familial hypercholesterolaemia. Hypercholesterolaemia is an inherited condition caused by a genetic fault. It leads to high cholesterol levels, even in people who have a healthy lifestyle.
How to take statins
Statins come as tablets that are taken once a day. The tablets should normally be taken at the same time each day. Most people take them before going to bed.
In most cases, you’ll have to take statins for life. This is because cholesterol levels rise if you stop taking the medication.
Before you start taking statins, your doctor should carry out a
blood test
to check the condition of your liver. You should also have a routine blood test to check the health of your liver 3 months after treatment begins, and another after 12 months.
Missed or extra doses
Missing any of your doses could make your treatment less effective.
If you ever forget to take your dose, don’t take an extra one to make up for it. Just take your next dose as usual the following day.
If you take more tablets than prescribed, you should speak to your pharmacist or GP practice. You can also phone 111 for advice.
Possible side effects
Like all medications, statins can cause side effects. Most people don’t experience any problems.
You should talk to your doctor if you have side effects after taking statins. Your dose may need to be adjusted or you may need a different type of statin.
Check the leaflet that comes with your medicine for information about its side effects.
Common side effects
Common side effects of statins can include:
nosebleeds
sore throat
a runny or blocked nose (non-allergic rhinitis)
headache
feeling sick
problems with the digestive system, like
constipation
,
diarrhoea
,
indigestion
or
flatulence
muscle and joint pain
increased blood sugar level (
hyperglycaemia
)
an increased risk of
diabetes
muscle tenderness or weakness
Less common side effects
Less common side effects of statins include:
being sick
loss of appetite
weight gain
difficulty sleeping (
insomnia
) or having nightmares
dizziness
loss of sensation or tingling in the nerve endings of the hands and feet (
peripheral neuropathy
)
memory problems
blurred vision
ringing in the ears
inflammation of the liver (hepatitis), which can cause
flu-like symptoms
inflammation of the pancreas (
pancreatitis
), which can cause
stomach pain
skin problems, like
acne
or an itchy red rash
feeling unusually tired or physically weak
Myopathy
Some people are at increased risk of developing a rare side effect called myopathy. Myopathy is where the tissues of your muscles become damaged and painful. It can lead to kidney damage (rhabdomyolysis).
Things that can increase this risk include:
being over 70 years old
having a history of liver disease
regularly drinking a lot of alcohol
having a history of muscle-related side effects when taking a statin or fibrate (another type of medicine for high cholesterol)
having a family history of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis
If one or more of these apply to you, you may need to be monitored more often to check for complications. A lower dose of statin may also be recommended.
Warnings and precautions
Statins may not be suitable if you have severe liver disease, or blood tests suggest that your liver may not be working properly. Statins can affect your liver, and this is more likely to cause serious problems if you already have a severely damaged liver.
If you have an
underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
, this would be treated first. Having an underactive thyroid can lead to an increased cholesterol level. Treating hypothyroidism may cause your cholesterol level to decrease without needing statins. Statins are also more likely to cause muscle damage in people with an underactive thyroid.
Other medicines and statins
Medications that can interact with some types of statin include:
certain
antibiotics
and antifungals
certain
HIV
medications
warfarin
– used to prevent blood clots
ciclosporin – used to treat conditions including
psoriasis
and
rheumatoid arthritis
danazol – used to treat conditions such as
endometriosis
verapamil and diltiazem – used to treat conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels
amiodarone – used to treat irregular heartbeats
fibrates – help to reduce cholesterol levels in the blood
If you are taking statins and need to take one of these medications, your doctor may prescribe an alternative or lower dosage. In some cases, they may recommend that you temporarily stop taking your statin.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
You shouldn’t take statins if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding. There’s no firm evidence on whether it’s safe to do so.
If you do become pregnant while taking statins, contact your GP for advice.
Food and drink
Grapefruit juice can affect some statins and increase your risk of side effects. Your doctor may advise you to avoid it or to only consume it in small amounts.
There are no known interactions between statins and alcohol.
Alternatives to statins
If you’re at risk of CVD, your doctor will recommend that you make lifestyle changes before you take statins. If lifestyle changes don’t help, statins may be recommended.
Lifestyle changes can include:
eating a
healthy, balanced diet
exercising regularly
maintaining a healthy weight
limiting the amount of alcohol you drink
stopping smoking
